sources.title: Illinois State Museum, The Illinois
sources.note: Overview and evidence menu distinguish Illinois identity, lifeways, history, archaeology, and the limits of written records.

sources.title: Illinois State Museum, Identity
sources.note: Lines 7 to 12: several independent Illinois tribes shared a language, lifeways, and territory; Kaskaskia was one principal tribe.

sources.title: Illinois State Museum, Territory
sources.note: Lines 4 to 6: initial-contact Illinois Country and distinct locations, with Kaskaskia in the upper Illinois River valley.

sources.title: Illinois State Museum, Written Records
sources.note: Lines 4 to 7: Marquette visited in 1673 and 1675; Delliette lived among Kaskaskia and Peoria from 1687 to 1698 and wrote about 1702.

sources.title: Illinois State Museum, Ancestors of the Illinois Indians
sources.note: Lines 2 to 4: Danner pottery mismatch, tentative northern Ohio clues, and the explicit conclusion that ancestry remains open.

sources.title: Illinois State Museum, Zimmerman Site
sources.note: Lines 5 to 19: intermittent 1673 to 1691 occupation, multiple earlier occupations, artifacts, houses, possible sweat lodges, pits, foods, and fauna.

sources.title: Robert Mazrim, Protohistory at the Grand Village of the Kaskaskia: The Illinois Country on the Eve of Colony
sources.note: Illinois Experts lines 8 to 20 give the title, author, and abstract; lines 55 to 64 give the full citation for the 2015 Illinois State Archaeological Survey report focused on seventeenth-century contexts.

sources.title: A. J. White, Samuel E. Munoz, Sissel Schroeder, and Lora R. Stevens, “After Cahokia: Indigenous Repopulation and Depopulation of the Horseshoe Lake Watershed AD 1400–1900”
sources.note: Cambridge lines 437 to 447 give the exact title and authors; lines 487 to 495 give the abstract; lines 654 to 659 address persistence and the conclusion.

sources.title: Illinois State Museum, Exploration
sources.note: Lines 6 to 14: Marquette and Jolliet in 1673, a 74-cabin Kaskaskia village, later aggregation, council, food, and French contact.

sources.title: Illinois State Museum, Settlements
sources.note: Lines 2 to 6: 1677 village count and later-documented summer villages, bison camps, and smaller winter villages.

sources.title: Illinois State Museum, Houses
sources.note: Lines 5 to 11: later-recorded longhouses, family quarters, central hearths, winter wigwams, reed mats, construction, and water resistance.

sources.title: Illinois State Museum, Food
sources.note: Lines 4 to 6: Marquette 1674 account, mixed hunting, fishing, gathering, agriculture, divided work, and early eighteenth-century change.

sources.title: Illinois State Museum, Division of Labor
sources.note: Lines 6 to 9: historically documented hunting, trade, farming, food processing, building, craft, child raising, and leadership roles.

sources.title: Illinois State Museum, Tools and Utensils
sources.note: Line 30: tools made from wood, bone, antler, shell, and stone are known from French documents and archaeology.

sources.title: Illinois State Museum, Containers
sources.note: Lines 25 to 29: Zimmerman pottery, shell temper, paddle and anvil shaping, firing, water carrying, cooking, cloth, and medicine bags.

sources.title: Illinois State Museum, Transportation
sources.note: Lines 4 to 9: later evidence for walking, cottonwood dugouts, household hauling, and horses reaching Kaskaskia in 1711.

sources.title: Illinois State Museum, European Trade Goods
sources.note: Lines 4 to 15: seventeenth-century trade, continued bows, brass-kettle reuse, iron tools, cloth, beads, and ornaments.

sources.title: Illinois State Museum, Family
sources.note: Lines 4 to 6: Delliette around 1702 describes marriage ages, consent, family gift exchanges, and lodge residence.

sources.title: Illinois State Museum, Society
sources.note: Lines 4 to 7: later accounts of egalitarian access, consensus, persuasive chiefs, and colonial centralization after the late 1600s.

sources.title: Illinois State Museum, Leaders
sources.note: Lines 4 to 8: 1673 village leadership, peace and war chiefs, limited authority, women leaders, feasts, gifts, and accountability.

sources.title: Illinois State Museum, Health
sources.note: Lines 4 to 8: Allouez 1667 and Delliette 1702 accounts of healers, family payment, plant medicines, and explicitly uncertain plant identifications.

sources.title: Illinois State Museum, Beliefs
sources.note: Lines 4 to 9: later-recorded ritual and daily life, hunting and healing, a 1693 elder, and missionary pressure.

sources.title: Illinois State Museum, Death
sources.note: Lines 5 to 11: Delliette 1702 on mourning, family gifts, burial crews and objects, beliefs, and commemorative recreation.

sources.title: Illinois State Museum, Lacrosse
sources.note: Lines 28 to 31: Delliette 1702 describes mixed-village teams of men and women, rackets, wooden ball, and scoring.

sources.title: Illinois State Museum, Straw Game
sources.note: Lines 28 to 38: Delliette 1702 and the reconstructed counting, guessing, seed scoring, wagering, and six-based remainder play.

sources.title: Illinois State Museum, Decorative Art
sources.note: Lines 28 to 39: later-attributed hide paintings, weaving, dyes, quillwork, carving, recurring colors, mats, and surviving objects.

sources.title: Illinois State Museum, The Illinois Today
sources.note: Lines 4 to 11: Kaskaskia and Peoria survival, nineteenth-century unions and removals, living Peoria government, gatherings, and community programs.

sources.title: Peewaalia Language and Cultural Education portal
sources.note: Lines 61 to 64 give the exact sample and translation; lines 94 to 119 describe revitalization and family, elder, youth, and community learning.

sources.title: Peoria Tribe, About Peewaalia
sources.note: Lines 65 to 90, 100 to 103, and 115 to 144: community identity, four roots including Kaskaskia, settler pressure, community interpretation, language history, modern writing, learning, and continuity.

sources.title: Peoria Tribe, Culture and Language
sources.note: Lines 19 to 60: eleven-week in-person and online courses teach pronunciation, daily vocabulary, listening, reading, and writing.

sources.title: Peoria Tribe Early Childhood Program
sources.note: Mission and services: family partnership, heritage, language, childcare, curriculum, screenings, tutoring, nutrition, conferences, and monthly family meetings.

sources.title: Peoria Tribe, Indian Child Welfare
sources.note: Mission and services: protect children, preserve families, prevent breakup, support reunification and adoption, and certify foster homes.

sources.title: Peoria Tribe, Health and Human Services
sources.note: Department page lists health, safety, food assistance, mental health, recovery, domestic concerns, child welfare, and family support.

sources.title: Peoria Tribe, Government
sources.note: Lines 18 to 33 link the elected Business Committee, constitution, ordinances, elections, committees, and official meeting records.

sources.title: United States Statutes at Large, “A Treaty Between the United States of America and the Kaskaskia Tribe of Indians” (1803)
sources.note: Exact formal heading at 7 Stat. 78, lines 0 to 23; 7 Stat. 78 to 79, Articles 1 to 7 cover cession, reserve, annuity, house, field, children’s instruction, boundary claim, and hunting.

sources.title: United States Statutes at Large, “Treaty with the Kaskaskias, Etc.” (1832)
sources.note: Exact running heading at 7 Stat. 403, line 0; 7 Stat. 403 to 405, Articles I to VIII cover union, cessions, Kansas land, annuity, houses, equipment, movement, and signatory marks.

sources.title: United States Statutes at Large, “Treaty with the Kaskaskias, &c.” (May 30, 1854)
sources.note: Exact running heading at 10 Stat. 1082, line 0; 10 Stat. 1082 to 1087, especially Articles 1 to 3, cover the Kaskaskia, Peoria, Piankeshaw, and Wea confederation and Kansas cession.

sources.title: Lenville J. Stelle and Parkland College Anthropology Students, “Inoca (Ilimouec, Illinois, Illini, Peoria) Ethnohistory Project: Eye Witness Descriptions of the Contact Generation, 1667–1700”
sources.note: Page lines 0 to 8 give the exact title, creator, and date; lines 26 to 40 explain that contact accounts are incomplete, subjective, racist, and one-sided because the project lacks Inoca community voices.
